title: Johor Data Centres Power Demand Forecast – Rising Trends
abstract: Johor's data centre boom is rewriting the region's power playbook, and the numbers are eye-opening.
body:
## The Power Crunch in Johor

Johor's data centre scene is booming, and that means one thing: a whole lot of electricity is about to be needed. According to a fresh forecast, the power demand from these facilities is set to climb steeply in the coming years. The source article lays out the numbers, and they're not small. By 2035, data centres in Johor are expected to draw 5.5 gigawatts of power. That's a massive jump from the 1.2 gigawatts they consumed in 2024. To put it another way, the demand is projected to more than quadruple over that stretch. The forecast points to a compound annual growth rate of 15 percent, which is the kind of pace that gets utilities and planners reaching for their spreadsheets.

## Why the Ramp-Up Is So Steep

The article explains that this surge isn't just a random spike. It's driven by the usual suspects: cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and the general digitisation of everything. Johor has become a magnet for data centre investment thanks to its proximity to Singapore, relatively cheaper land and power, and supportive government policies. But all that growth comes with a catch. The forecast warns that if the power infrastructure doesn't keep up, the boom could hit a wall. The source notes that the current grid capacity in Johor is around 3 gigawatts, which means the projected 5.5 gigawatts by 2035 would blow past what's available today. That gap is the central tension of the story.

## The Grid Gap and What It Means

The article doesn't shy away from the challenges. It points out that while the demand forecast is eye-catching, the real question is whether the supply side can match it. Johor's grid is already feeling the strain, and the forecast suggests that without significant upgrades, the region could face reliability issues. The source mentions that the state government and utility companies are aware of the problem and are working on plans to expand capacity. But those plans take time, and data centres don't wait around. The article hints that some operators might have to look at alternative solutions, like on-site generation or energy storage, to bridge the gap. It's a classic race between demand and infrastructure.

## Regional Ripples and the Singapore Factor

The forecast also touches on the broader regional context. Johor's data centre growth is closely tied to Singapore, which has imposed a moratorium on new data centres due to its own land and power constraints. That has pushed a lot of demand across the border. The source article notes that this dynamic is unlikely to change soon, which means Johor's power demand will keep climbing. It also mentions that other countries in the region, like Malaysia and Indonesia, are watching closely. If Johor can't meet the demand, the investment could flow elsewhere. The article suggests that the next few years will be critical in determining whether Johor becomes a true data centre hub or just a temporary overflow valve.

## What to Watch Going Forward

The source wraps up by listing a few key things to keep an eye on. First, whether the planned grid upgrades actually materialise on schedule. Second, how quickly data centre operators adopt more efficient technologies that could temper demand growth. Third, whether government policies continue to favour data centre investment or shift towards stricter energy requirements. The article doesn't make predictions beyond the forecast, but it does make clear that the 5.5 gigawatt figure by 2035 is not a given. It's a projection based on current trends, and trends can change. Still, if the past few years are any guide, Johor's power demand from data centres is only heading in one direction: up. The article ends with a note that stakeholders should prepare for a future where data centres are among the largest electricity consumers in the state, and that planning needs to start now.

That's the gist of the source. The numbers are big, the challenges are real, and the clock is ticking. Whether Johor can pull it off is the million-dollar question, or maybe the multi-gigawatt one.
